[1;97mMODULE — env: variables and the prompt[0m

Five short lessons, then a gate. This module stands alone and saves
nothing. Type [92mquit[0m to leave at any point.

You will see:
  variables, and how the shell uses them
  [92mexport[0m, and what a child program receives
  [92mPATH[0m, the list the shell searches for programs
  the prompt, which is a variable too
  where these settings live for real

Everything stays inside this tutor's practice shell. Your own
configuration files are not touched.

[93m▶ Type [92mnext[93m to begin lesson 1.[0m
[95mnext[0m[90m ▸ go on[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ this screen again[0m   [95mprev[0m[90m ▸ back[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97menv 1 — variables[0m

A [36mvariable[0m is a name that holds a value. The shell swaps
[92m$name[0m for the value before it runs the line.

  [92mecho $HOME[0m           [90m# a variable the shell already has[0m
  [92mpet=owl[0m               [90m# set one: no spaces around =[0m
  [92mecho $pet[0m            [90m# prints owl[0m
  [92menv | head[0m            [90m# the first lines of the variable list[0m
  [92menv | grep '^pet='[0m    [90m# prints nothing[0m

Notice that [92mpet[0m is missing from the list. A variable you set
is private to this shell until you export it (lesson 2).

[93m▶ Try the five lines, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m
[95mnext[0m[90m ▸ go on[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ this screen again[0m   [95mprev[0m[90m ▸ back[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97menv 2 — export and child programs[0m

A program the shell starts is a [36mchild[0m. It receives only the
variables that were [36mexported[0m. Single quotes stop this shell from
replacing [92m$pet[0m, so the child does it.

  [92mpet=owl[0m                          [90m# set it again: new screen, new shell[0m
  [92mbash -c 'echo [$pet]'[0m            [90m# prints [] : the child sees nothing[0m
  [92mexport pet[0m                       [90m# mark it for children[0m
  [92mbash -c 'echo [$pet]'[0m            [90m# prints [owl][0m
  [92menv | grep '^pet='[0m               [90m# now it is listed[0m

Notice that [92mexport[0m copies nothing. It marks the name so every
child gets the value at the moment it starts.

[93m▶ Run the five lines in order, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m
[95mnext[0m[90m ▸ go on[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ this screen again[0m   [95mprev[0m[90m ▸ back[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97menv 3 — PATH is a list[0m

[92mPATH[0m is a variable that holds folders separated by [92m:[0m. When you
type a command name, the shell looks in those folders, in order, and
runs the first match.

  [92mecho "$PATH"[0m                  [90m# one long line[0m
  [92mecho "$PATH" | tr : '\n'[0m      [90m# one folder per line[0m
  [92mcommand -v ls[0m                 [90m# the folder where ls was found[0m

This is why [92mcommand -v[0m (Stage 4) could answer: it reads this list.
A program in a folder that is not on the list is not found by name.

[93m▶ Run the three lines, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m
[95mnext[0m[90m ▸ go on[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ this screen again[0m   [95mprev[0m[90m ▸ back[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97menv 4 — the prompt is a variable[0m

The text before your cursor is the variable [92mPS1[0m. Change it and the
prompt changes at once.

  [92mPS1='me> '[0m       [90m# the prompt is now me>[0m
  [92mPS1='$ '[0m         [90m# and now a plain dollar sign[0m

Try both. Then type [92mnext[0m and look at the prompt on the next screen.

[93m▶ Change the prompt, then type [92mnext[93m.[0m
[95mnext[0m[90m ▸ go on[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ this screen again[0m   [95mprev[0m[90m ▸ back[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97menv 5 — where this lives for real[0m

Your prompt went back: each screen starts a fresh shell, and the tutor
ignores your own configuration files so every learner sees the same thing.
A real terminal reads one file when it starts:
  [94m~/.bashrc[0m   if your login shell is bash
  [94m~/.zshrc[0m    if it is zsh [90m(check: echo $SHELL)[0m
[90mmacOS with bash reads ~/.bash_profile instead.[0m

Lines you could add there:
  [92mPS1='$ '[0m
  [92mexport PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"[0m

[91mQuit the tutor[0m, open a new terminal, edit the file there. The tutor
will not touch it. Open another new terminal to see the change.

[1;97menv — gate[0m

[36mRecall[0m (three questions, all three must be correct).
Then a [36mpractical task[0m.
[93m┃[0m [96mQ1: Which command makes a variable visible to the programs the shell starts?  (set, export, env, echo)[0m

[93m┃[0m [96mQ2: What does [92mPATH[0m hold?  (a list of folders, one folder, a file name)[0m
[93m┃[0m [92manswer in words:[0m
[93m┃[0m [96mQ3: You type [92mPS1='me> '[0m, then [92mnext[0m. What is the prompt on the next screen?  (me> , shelltutor> )[0m

[1;97menv — task[0m

Prove that a child program can see a variable you exported. You will
work inside [94m/var/folders/jx/f_4n055973x5cwnyh_mhlw9h0000gn/T/shelltutor-sim-home-sizxv_ci/env[0m.

  1. set [92mTOPIC[0m to the word [36mshell[0m
  2. export it
  3. run a child [92mbash -c[0m that prints [92m$TOPIC[0m into [94mseen.txt[0m
     [90m(hint: single quotes, so the child replaces the variable)[0m

[90mI will check: seen.txt holds the word shell, and your history shows[0m
[90mTOPIC set, exported, and read inside single quotes by a child.[0m

[93m▶ Type [92mcheck[93m when done.[0m
[95mcheck[0m[90m ▸ test your work[0m   [95mshow[0m[90m ▸ the task again[0m   [95mquit[0m[90m ▸ save and leave[0m

[1;97m✓ env cleared.[0m

Commands and keys from this module:
  [92mname=value    [0m [90mset a variable in this shell[0m
  [92mexport name   [0m [90mlet child programs see it[0m

  [92menv           [0m [90mlist what children receive[0m
